newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Eighty years on, Lenin still stirs Russian passion.
newsitem.headline: Eighty years on, Lenin still stirs Russian passion.

text.p: Vladimir Lenin had a talent for stirring up political passions. As an atheist, he might be surprised to find he has not lost it, 73 years after his death.

Boris Yeltsin wants to put the Bolshevik leader's mummified body at the heart of a new battle with his communist opponents in the Russian parliament. The president on Friday resurrected his idea of holding a referendum on finally burying the corpse.
"Let the people decide whether to bury him in a Christian way or leave things as they are," he said in St Petersburg, cradle of the Russian Revolution 80 years ago and once called Leningrad.
It immediately ran into howls of rage from the opposition, as Yeltsin must have known it would.
"This may provoke a major social conflict," senior communist legislator Viktor Ilyukhin told reporters.

The communist-dominated parliament, which still reveres the founder of the Soviet state, already passed a bill this week banning architectural changes in Red Square, where Lenin's body lies along the Kremlin wall in a red marble mausoleum.
Yeltsin, back in fighting form after illness and pushing liberal reforms harder than ever before, is likely to ignore it -- another reminder of who holds real power in Russia.

At stake in a referendum is not so much the mortal remains and disputed last wishes of Lenin himself, who died of a stroke in 1924 at the age of 53, seven years after leading the coup d'etat that brought the Bolsheviks to power.
"This country has more troubles and worries than the funeral of a mummified body," liberal legislator Vladimir Lukin said.

The heart of the matter is Lenin's political legacy, the seven decades after the revolution which Yeltsin and his liberal allies have roundly rejected but which the communist and nationalist opposition believes is still a model for the future.
As nationalist parliamentarian Sergei Baburin put it: "Yeltsin's suggestion is a bluff. The referendum on Lenin's body may turn into a referendum on Yeltsin's political fate."

The call for the plebiscite -- which communists say they would win easily -- comes at a time of mounting tension in Russia's uneasily balanced political system, between the Kremlin and parliament. Rumours are rife Yeltsin may dissolve the lower house, the State Duma, if it continues to block economic reforms.
Analysts say the government has little to gain from new elections, with voters angry at continuing economic crisis. They suggest such speculation is simply a way of exerting pressure on the Duma.

Raising the prospect of a referendum could be a part of that pressure, bringing with it the possibility the Kremlin might use the vote to seek public backing to overcome Duma opposition. In 1993, Yeltsin won support in a referendum. Months later he shelled the recalcitrant Soviet-era parliament into submission.
It was at that time that the issue of Lenin's body last featured so high on the political agenda. Then, Yeltsin said the embalmed revolutionary would be given a Christian burial within weeks.
Somehow, though, the matter was shelved.

The case for ousting Lenin from Red Square, where his goateed, sobre-suited mummy is still on show, ranges from liberals who view his rule as cruel and disastrous for Russia to those who argue that Lenin himself wanted only to be buried
